title: Which practice answers which question?
blurb: Read a concern in the scenario, name the question behind it and match it to the practice that handles it in an agile project.
question: At Pinewick Home and Garden, the head of internal audit asks how the board will know, between stage boundaries, whether the click and collect project is still on track. Which practice deals with this concern?

teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile keeps all seven practices: business case, organization, plans, quality, risk, issues and progress. Each keeps its PRINCE2 purpose; the agile book then shows which management products to keep, tailor or replace with agile artifacts. In the exam, a scenario rarely names the practice. It describes a worry, and you must spot the question behind it and match it to the right practice.

teach.h: The practices and their agile forms
head: Practice
Core question or purpose
Agile form
rows: Why does it exist; what must it stay aligned to?
What, who, how, where, when, how much?
What is acceptable to users; how is it measured?
What now, when a product deviates?
Are we on track; control any exception
teach.caption: Business case, quality, risk and issues questions are from Table 5.2; the organization, plans and progress lines are shorthand from their purposes (7.1, 8.1, 12.1).

teach.body: Business case: judge whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable. Organization: set up the structure of accountability and responsibilities. Plans: define the products and the means to deliver them, with estimates of time and cost. Quality: document users' requirements of the products and how they will be met. Risk: identify, assess and control uncertainty. Issues: assess issues and control changes to the baseline. Progress: compare actuals with plans, forecast, and control deviations causing an exception.

teach.h: Name the question, then the practice

root.label: What is the scenario worried about?

teach.caption: Tense matters: an uncertain future event is risk; something that has happened, or a request to change the baseline, is an issue.
Progress also controls deviations that cause an exception (12.1).

teach.text: Watch the near misses. 'Control changes to the baseline' is the issues practice, but 'control any deviations causing an exception' is the progress practice. Defining what is acceptable to users is quality; dealing with a product that turns out not to meet it is issues.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pinewick click and collect
teach.body: Project manager Patrick Dunne sorts the board's concerns. The finance director wants evidence that sales will rise, not just move channel: business case. The head of store operations insists stock accuracy reaches 97% before a store goes live: quality. Tallis Logistics may not fit its quarterly release cycle to the project: risk. Internal audit asks how the board will know, between stage boundaries, whether the project is on track: progress, answered by the project dashboard.

teach.h: Four steps for a 'which practice' question

steps.label: Find the concern
steps.sub: What is the person actually worried about?

steps.label: Turn it into a question
steps.sub: Why, who, what or when, good enough, what if, what now, on track

steps.label: Match the practice
steps.sub: Use the purpose, not a keyword in the stem

steps.label: Check the artifact
steps.sub: Canvas, release map, DoD, Agilometer, dashboard

rows.label: Who may approve a change to the store roll-out order?
How many releases, when, and with which features?
Lockers will not fit at three of the 20 largest stores
Is the project still worth its £1.6 million?

teach.note: The board already agreed that lockers may go in at fewer stores, so the locker problem is handled as an issue within agreed limits.

items: All seven practices remain; agile changes how they are applied, not why (Table 5.2).
Business case: worth it? Organization: who? Plans: what, how, when, how much?
Quality: what is acceptable and how is it measured?
Risk: what if (uncertain future). Issues: what now (has happened, or a baseline change).
Progress: actual against plan, forecasts, and control of deviations causing an exception.

summary: You can now turn a concern in the scenario into the question behind it and match it to the right practice. You can also separate the classic near misses: risk against issues, issues against progress, and quality against issues.

A.q: At Larkspur Rail, a board member asks whether the expected benefits of the Fair Fares project still outweigh its £3.2 million cost, now that the contract penalties have been reduced. Which practice addresses this concern?
A.why: Whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable, weighing costs against benefits, is the business case question: why does the project exist and what must it stay aligned to (6.1, Table 5.2).

whyNot.0: Organization sets up the structure of accountability and responsibilities; it does not judge whether the investment is justified.
whyNot.2: Risk deals with uncertain events that might affect objectives; this is a judgement about overall justification.
whyNot.3: Quality deals with what is acceptable to users and how it is measured, not whether the investment is worthwhile.

A.q: At Callowmere University, the web team and the Northmere Systems team say it is unclear who may set priorities across both teams and to whom each product owner reports. Which practice should resolve this?
A.why: The organization practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities: the 'who' (7.1).

whyNot.0: Plans define the products and the means to deliver them; they draw on the roles but do not establish them.
whyNot.1: The business case judges whether the project is worth doing; it does not define reporting lines or decision rights.
whyNot.2: Issues handles events and changes to the baseline; unclear roles are a structural matter for organization.

A.q: At Draycott Precision Engineering, Senticore warns that a component shortage could stretch its ten-week sensor lead time. The project manager wants to assess this and plan a response before anything goes wrong. Which practice is she applying?
A.why: A possible future event with an uncertain effect on objectives is a risk. The risk practice identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty (10.1, 5.3.1).

whyNot.1: Issues deals with events that have already happened or requests to change the baseline; the shortage has not happened.
whyNot.2: Progress compares actuals with plans; nothing has yet deviated.
whyNot.3: Plans set out what will be delivered and when; responding to an uncertain event is risk work.

B.q: During Release 1 at Easterholm County Council, testers find that the carers' self-assessment will not meet the easy-read criteria agreed for it. Which practice deals with what happens next?
B.why: A product that will not meet its agreed specification is an off-specification, one of the issue types. The issues practice answers 'what now, when a product deviates from what was agreed?' (11.3.1, Table 5.2).

whyNot.0: Quality defined the easy-read criteria in the first place; handling a product that fails them is an issue.
whyNot.1: Risk handles uncertain future events; this shortfall has already been found.
whyNot.2: Progress tracks plan against actual; a specific product deviation is captured and assessed as an issue.

B.q: At Pinewick, the head of internal audit asks how the board will know between stage boundaries whether the project is on track and whether a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded. Which practice answers this?
B.why: Progress monitors and compares actual achievement against plan, forecasts objectives, and controls deviations causing an exception (12.1). In agile this is mainly through the project dashboard pulled by the board.

whyNot.0: Issues controls changes to the baseline; the auditor is asking about ongoing monitoring and forecasting.
whyNot.2: Plans set the baseline to measure against; checking actuals against it is progress.
whyNot.3: The business case judges justification; the auditor is asking how the board tracks performance.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's tenants' panel asks how the project will decide whether online repair reporting is good enough for older tenants, and how that will be measured. Which practice addresses this?
B.why: Quality documents users' requirements of the products and how they will be met. Its question is what is acceptable to the users and how it can be measured (9.1, Table 5.2).

whyNot.0: The business case judges whether the project is worthwhile, not the acceptance standard of a product.
whyNot.1: Issues would apply once a product deviates from agreed criteria; here the criteria are still being set.
whyNot.3: Plans define what will be delivered and when; acceptance criteria and measurement belong to quality.

C.q: At Larkspur Rail, Coinbridge Payments tells the project manager that its payment team has been disbanded and work on automatic payment has stopped. He records this in the risk register and plans to discuss it at the next retrospective. Is this an appropriate application of the risk practice, and why?
options: Yes, because risks are identified in every retrospective
Yes, because the risk register records threats to objectives
No, because an event that has happened is handled as an issue
No, because supplier matters belong in the commercial approach
C.why: The stoppage has already happened, so it is a problem (an issue type), handled by the issues practice: capture, assess and respond. Risk deals with uncertain future events (11.3.1, Table 5.2).

whyNot.0: Risk identification is part of retrospectives (10.3.1), but that does not make a past event a risk.
whyNot.1: The register does hold threats, but this is no longer uncertain; it has happened.
whyNot.3: The commercial management approach covers procurement and contracts, not the handling of an event that has stopped work.

C.q: At Callowmere University, the ethics review may delay the early-warning feature. The project manager updates the project canvas with best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios and treats this as business case work. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the canvas tailors the business case with three cases
Yes, because the chief product owner owns the project backlog
No, because the canvas is an artifact of the plans practice
No, because benefits are confirmed after the project closes
C.why: In PRINCE2 Agile the business case is tailored to the project canvas, which should outline best-case, worst-case and expected-case scenarios (Table 5.2). Updating it for a possible delay keeps the justification current.

whyNot.1: True, but backlog ownership does not explain why canvas updates are business case work.
whyNot.2: The project canvas belongs to the business case practice (6.3.2); the release map is the plans artifact.
whyNot.3: Confirming benefits mostly happens after closure, but the canvas is still kept current during the project.

C.q: Draycott's budget and end date are fixed. The project manager uses a release-level burn-up chart, reviewed at each progress review, to forecast whether Release 2 will be complete in time. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because burn charts show the total exposure to risk
Yes, because it compares actual with planned work and forecasts
No, because zero time tolerance makes tracking pointless
No, because forecasting completion is part of the plans practice
C.why: Progress monitors actual against planned achievement and forecasts objectives (12.1). With what is delivered as the main flexible aspect, burn charts suit every level (12.3.1).

whyNot.0: Total risk exposure is shown by a cumulative risk burn-down chart, a risk technique, not a burn-up of work.
whyNot.2: Tracking spend or time against a zero tolerance adds little, but tracking how much scope is delivered is exactly what burn charts are for.
whyNot.3: Plans set the baseline; monitoring and forecasting against it during delivery is progress.

reteach.title: A building job with seven questions
reteach.question: Imagine renovating a house. Which question would each of the seven practices ask?

blocks.body: Is the extension worth the money (business case)? Who decides and who does the work (organization)? What gets built, in what order, by when and for how much (plans)? What standard must the kitchen meet, and how will we check it (quality)? What if the supplier is late (risk)? The worktop arrived cracked: what now (issues)? Are we on schedule, and will we breach the budget limit (progress)?

blocks.text: Something that might happen is risk. Something that has happened, or a request to change the baseline, is an issue.

explain.body: The business case asks whether the project is and remains desirable, viable and achievable, so it is worth investing in. Organization sets out who is accountable and who is responsible, through roles, team structure and decision rights.

test.q: At Saltmarsh Housing Group, nobody is sure who should settle priority clashes between the service design team and the digital team. Which practice should address this?
test.why: Deciding who holds authority for priorities across teams is part of the structure of accountability and responsibilities defined by the organization practice (7.1, 7.3.1).

whyNot.0: The business case judges justification, not who settles priorities.
whyNot.2: Issues handles events and baseline changes, not standing decision rights.
whyNot.3: Plans set out what is delivered and when, not who has authority.

explain.h: What, when, and is it good enough?
explain.body: Plans define the products and the means to deliver them: who, how, where, when and how much; in agile the release map is the project and stage plan. Quality documents what users need from the products and how it will be met and measured, through the backlogs, DoR and DoD.

test.q: Pinewick's project manager must show the board how many releases there will be, when each lands and which features each holds, with the budget referenced. Which practice is he applying?
test.why: The release map serves as the project and stage plan: how many releases, when, and which features, with budget, tolerances and assumptions included or referenced (Table 8.1).

whyNot.1: Progress compares actuals with this plan later; producing the plan is plans work.
whyNot.2: Quality sets acceptance criteria, not release timing and content.
whyNot.3: The business case justifies the investment; the release map is the plan.

explain.body: Risk handles uncertainty that would affect objectives: identify, assess, plan, implement, communicate. Issues handles what has happened or is requested: requests for change, off-specifications, problems and business opportunities, and controls changes to the baseline.

test.q: At Easterholm, Abacus Care Software says that if a change is needed to its interface, its six-week quoting time could delay Release 2. Which practice should handle this?
test.why: A possible future delay that depends on whether a change is needed is uncertain, so it is a risk to assess and respond to (10.1).

whyNot.0: No change has been requested and nothing has gone wrong yet, so it is not an issue.
whyNot.1: Progress compares actuals with plans; nothing has deviated.
whyNot.3: Organization defines roles; the delay is an uncertainty about delivery.

explain.body: Progress monitors and compares actual achievements with those planned, forecasts objectives and continued viability, and controls deviations that cause an exception. In agile, dashboards and burn charts carry most of this, and the board pulls information rather than waiting for long reports.

test.q: Callowmere's pro vice-chancellor asks how she can see each fortnight whether the forecast for Release 1 still sits within its tolerances. Which practice provides this?
test.why: Monitoring actual against plan and forecasting whether tolerances will hold is the progress practice (12.1), typically through the project dashboard.

whyNot.0: Plans give the baseline; checking against it each fortnight is progress.
whyNot.1: Risk handles uncertain events, not routine tracking of forecasts.
whyNot.2: The business case judges justification, not fortnightly status against tolerance.
